levels.8-10: A garden's dates are its fort's. It is drawn and named on the 1830 plan, and in 1831 someone walking by saw it full of fruit. So it was there on both sides of 1835. We end it when the soldiers left on 29 December 1836, not when the buildings were torn down. Soldiers kept the garden, and after that date there were none. Nothing tells what happened to it.

entries.card: notes:A NEGATIVE FINDING, RECORDED SO IT CANNOT BE UNDONE BY INFERENCE. The church had no tower. This is the same trap St Mary's carries in a sharper form - see that record, where a low open tower is attested at an undated 'some time afterwards' and would age the building forward if it were built - and it is recorded here because a visitor's expectation of what a church looks like is the strongest force acting on this model.

levels.8-10: A no, written down so no one adds one by guessing. The church had no tower. St. Mary's has the same trap: it got a low tower some time later, and building it would make that church look newer than 1835. We say so here because people expect a church to have a tower.

entries.card: notes:A PARTY OF FOUR WAGONS, invented: families came overland to Chicago from Indiana and Ohio in 1835 as well as by lake, and a party travelled together. L355.
entries.text: A PARTY OF FOUR WAGONS, invented: families came overland to Chicago from Indiana and Ohio in 1835 as well as by lake, and a party travelled together. L355.

levels.8-10: Four wagons in a group, our guess. In 1835, some families came to Chicago by land, from Indiana and Ohio. Others came by lake. A group went on the road together.

entries.card: notes:A PRICE DOCUMENTS A SERVICE; THE BUILDING IS THE INFERENCE. The Cook County Court of County Commissioners, sitting at Chicago on 13 April 1831, 'Ordered that the following rates be allowed to tavern keepers', among them 'For each horse fed 25' and 'Keeping horse one night 50' (Andreas, scan p. 249). That order set what a licensed Chicago house might charge to keep a traveller's horse; it is read here as standing for every public house the lodging model sizes, which is an inference, because no licence for this house in particular has been read. WHAT IT DOES NOT PROVE: a dedicated building. A horse can be kept at a picket line, in a fenced lot or at a livery up the street; this record draws the building because a house of this size on a Lake Street lot with an alley behind it is the ordinary case, and says so.

That order set what a licensed Chicago house might charge to keep a traveller's horse; it is read here as standing for every public house the lodging model sizes, which is an inference, because no licence for this house in particular has been read. WHAT IT DOES NOT PROVE: a dedicated building. A horse can be kept at a picket line, in a fenced lot or at a livery up the street; this record draws the building because a house of this size on a Lake Street lot with an alley behind it is the ordinary case, and says so.

levels.8-10: A price proves a service. The building is our guess. On 13 April 1831 the county set the prices tavern keepers could charge. Feeding a horse was 25 cents, and keeping a horse one night was 50 cents. We take that to cover every inn here. That is a guess, since we have not read this hotel's own license. It does not prove a stable. A horse can be tied to a rope, kept in a fenced lot, or kept up the street. We build a stable because a hotel this size, on a lot with an alley, usually had one.

entries.card: notes:A SQUARE OF ABOUT 53 m (174 ft), AND EVERY PART OF THAT SENTENCE HAS A DIFFERENT WARRANT. That it was SQUARE is Andreas in terms: 'The fort, as rebuilt, consisted of a square stockade inclosing barracks, quarters for the officers, magazine and provision-store' - and the 1830 plan agrees, drawing the two wall-to-wall distances within 3 percent of each other (161 and 157 pixels). THE SIZE IS DERIVED, NOT STATED. No source reached gives a dimension of this stockade; Quaife, who wrote the standing monograph on the fort and had the War Department files, prints Captain Whistler's measured 1808 draught of the FIRST fort and states no dimension of the second one anywhere. So 53 m is the 1830 plan measured at the scale that record's position note derives, and it carries +/-20 percent - the fort is somewhere between about 140 and 210 ft on a side. WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: the polygon is a rectangle because the plan draws a quadrangle, and nothing attests the corners were true or the sides equal to the foot.

entries.card: notes:A bounded July 1835 worksite, not a reconstruction of the completed hotel. Within the existing 24 × 15 m plan and 4 m maximum, 0.46 m thick brick walls now step down from the higher north working front to the lower rear lift. Two short timber working stages stand inside the shell. Bay count, wall thickness, lift heights, apertures, staging stock and placement are reconstructed working choices, not features traced from the later print. The existing external brick, timber and footing-stone piles remain separately declared in the yard layer. No excavation or below-grade interior is represented. L-lake-house-worksite-2379.

entries.card: notes:AN ADVERTISEMENT PROVES A TRADE, NOT A BUILDING, AND CERTAINLY NOT A BUILDING NINETEEN MONTHS LATER. That sentence is the source record's own warning about the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 and it is the whole difficulty with this record. What is documented is that Daniel Elston & Co. were carrying on a soap and candle manufactory in Chicago in November 1833, paying cash for tallow and house ashes; Andreas's summary of the paper's early advertising columns lists the same firm and trade (scan p. 755), which corroborates the advertisement and adds nothing to it. The range opens in November 1833 because that is the date of the copy, NOT because the works were built then — a manufactory that is advertising for raw material is already running. THE SURVIVAL TO 1835-07-01 IS AN ASSUMPTION AND THE CONFIDENCE SAYS SO: nothing reached follows this business past that advertisement, the scene date is nineteen months later in the fastest-changing period of the town's history, and the man himself is next seen in the sources decades on — an alderman in 1851, president of St George's Society in 1847, running the largest of Chicago's five brickyards by 1854 (Andreas scan pp. 389, 1073, 1169). A long career in the town is a reason to think he did not fail in 1834, and it is not evidence about a building. The range closes at the end of 1835 as the last date this record needs to claim.

levels.8-10: An ad proves a trade, not a building. Our own record warns of that, about the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833. We know Daniel Elston and partners made soap and candles in Chicago that November. They paid cash for tallow, which is animal fat, and for ashes from people's homes. A book lists the same business. We start in November 1833 because that is the ad's date. The works were already running then. That it lasted to July 1835 is a guess, and our confidence says so. Nothing follows the business after that ad. Elston shows up again years later, as a town leader and running the biggest brickyard by 1854. A long life in town hints he did not fail in 1834. That is not proof about a building. The record ends at the end of 1835.

entries.card: notes:ATTESTED FOR 1850 AND CARRIED BACK. Fergus: 'an 8-inch piece of square timber, imbedded in the earth, placed upright, about 2 feet high, upon the top of which was a brass plate on which had been a sun-dial'. Both dimensions built here are his. The date is the weakness - 'had been a sun-dial' is a man describing a relic in 1850, and nothing puts it on the parade in 1835 except that a post with a garrison has more use for a sun-dial than an abandoned one. WHERE IT STANDS IS OURS: Fergus puts his on a knoll near the southern end of a parade four hundred feet long, which is ground this record does not model, so the archetype stands it in the southern part of the court instead.

WHERE IT STANDS IS OURS: Fergus puts his on a knoll near the southern end of a parade four hundred feet long, which is ground this record does not model, so the archetype stands it in the southern part of the court instead.

entries.card: notes:Andreas dates the warehouse and slaughter yard to 1832 and gives no month, so the range opens at the start of that year. THE SURVIVAL TO THE SCENE DATE IS INFERENCE AND THERE IS A SPECIFIC REASON TO DOUBT IT: in 1834 Newberry and Dole built a slaughter-house on the South Branch, which is where a slaughtering business goes when it outgrows a yard behind a warehouse two blocks from the river. So at least half of what Andreas describes here had probably moved by the scene date. The warehouse itself is a different question and nothing reached follows it either way; it stands in this scene on the ordinary continuity argument. A LOCATION GUARD THAT MUST TRAVEL WITH THIS RECORD: Newberry and Dole's forwarding warehouse — the one at whose wharf the schooner Illinois was cheered on 12 July 1834 — was on the NORTH side of the river, immediately east of where Rush Street bridge later stood. This record is the separate SOUTH-side 1832 warehouse and slaughter yard. Do not merge them and do not move this one to the river.

entries.card: notes:Andreas says 'frame' and no more, and the word does not distinguish the two methods available. Balloon framing was developed in Chicago in 1832-33 and became the dominant local method within a few years; this building's date is not fixed and may precede that, so braced frame is the safer reading, exactly as the Sauganash record argues for 1831. The alternative is real and this note is where it is recorded rather than in a footnote: if the store went up in 1833 it could as easily have been balloon framed, and nothing reached decides it.

entries.card: notes:Andreas, 'Chicago from 1833 to 1837', vol. 1 p. 128, describing the town a visitor would have seen: 'It did not show a single steeple nor a chimney four feet above any roof. A flagstaff at the fort, some fifty feet high, flaunted, in pleasant weather and on holidays - a weather-beaten flag, as an emblem of civilization, patriotic pride, national domain, or anything else that might stir hearts of the denizens of the town.' It is not the 'Such was the old Fort previous to 1812' passage, it is not Whistler's 1808 index, and it is not a plate; it is Andreas's own narrative of the years the scene date sits in.

entries.card: notes:Andreas, of the rebuilt fort: 'was defended by bastions at the northwest and southeast angles. The block-house was in the southwest corner.' The 1830 plan draws a work at exactly three angles and leaves the north-east plain. GUARD: the widely repeated 'two blockhouses, one on the south-east corner, the other at the north-west' belongs to the FIRST fort - the passage it comes from ends 'Such was the old Fort previous to 1812' - and applying it here is the commonest error about this building.

entries.card: notes:Andreas: Carpenter 'purchased a lot on South Water Street, between LaSalle and Wells streets' and 'erected a small store' in the summer of 1833. The range opens at 1 August, the middle of that summer, because no month is given and a mid-season date claims less than either end of it. THE SURVIVAL TO THE SCENE DATE IS THE ORDINARY CONTINUITY ARGUMENT, and it is stronger here than on most records in this parcel: this is the building Carpenter MOVED INTO, two years old on the scene date, on the street he had just bought a lot on, and nothing suggests a man does that and then leaves. Carpenter's own advertisement in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 — drugs, medicines, oils, paints, dye-stuffs, and also dry groceries, glass and nails — shows him trading three months after building it, though it gives no address and so cannot say which of his two premises it was placed from. THE END IS A HOUSEKEEPING BOUND at the scene year, not a demolition date.

entries.card: notes:Attested standing in 1831 by Juliette Kinzie and by nobody else at any date. The range opens with the fort and closes at the final evacuation, because a root house is kept by a garrison; nothing reached follows it further.

entries.card: notes:Attested twice in Andreas, in two chapters, with dates either side of the scene date: 'In August of 1834, Mr. and Mrs. Murphy took charge of this new hotel, which they christened the Exchange Coffee House. They remained there until 1836, when they removed to the old Sauganash, the name of which they changed to United States Hotel'; and, in the life of Mark Beaubien, the house was 'first kept by Mr. and Mrs. John Murphy'. So 1835-07-01 falls inside their tenancy with eleven months either side, which makes this the best-attested occupancy in the parcel. A CONFLICT WORTH RECORDING RATHER THAN RESOLVING: this project's dossiers have Abram A. Markle 'associated from 1835-36' with the house, and the American's advertisement of August 1836 does call it 'Markle's Exchange Coffee House'. Andreas has Markle taking the MANSION HOUSE in 1835 and keeping it two years. Either Markle held both houses, or one of the two datings is loose; the Murphy tenancy is the one with dates on both sides of the scene date and it is what this record carries.

levels.8-10: A book says so twice, with dates on both sides of July 1835. It says the Murphys took over the new hotel in August 1834 and stayed until 1836. Then they moved to the old Sauganash. So July 1835 falls in their time, with eleven months on each side. That makes this the best-known stay in this part of town. One record does not agree. Our notes link Abram A. Markle to the house in 1835 and 1836, and an 1836 ad calls it Markle's Exchange Coffee House. But the book says Markle ran a different hotel in 1835. Either he ran both, or one date is loose. We keep the Murphys, since their dates are on both sides.

entries.card: notes:BUILT IN THE SPRING OF 1835, WHICH IS INSIDE THE SCENE YEAR AND BEFORE THE SCENE DATE. Andreas: 'In the spring of 1835, he built a house on what he supposed was his lot, only to find that he was on Monroe Street, not Adams, whither he proceeded to remove it on rollers.' The house, its season, its owner and the fact that it was moved a block are all documented. The range opens on 1835-03-01 as the earliest reading of 'the spring'.

entries.card: notes:Both halves are attested and they are attested separately. The store: Peck was a licensed merchant advertising dry goods, hardware and groceries through 1834-35. entries.card: notes:Both sources name Davis as the keeper in 1835, and Andreas's list of the Chicago American's advertising patrons carries 'John Davis, Steamboat Hotel' in the paper's first year. THE GRAIN IS THE YEAR, NOT THE DAY: DRLOIH has J. Dorsey and J. Force taking over the management on 9 November 1835, so Davis's tenure covers the scene date if the house was open at all. Note the coincidence this project should not resolve by assumption: a 'Mr. Davis' also took over the Sauganash Hotel in 1835, and whether that is the same John Davis is unattested.

entries.card: notes:Both witnesses give it the same double use and disagree only on which came first: chicagology says Walker erected it 'for a place of worship, and for a school house'; Wau-Bun says it was 'originally designed for a school-house, but occasionally used as a place of worship whenever any itinerant minister presented himself'. Either way, on 1835-07-01 it is the settlement's only building put up for worship or teaching. Jesse Walker himself died in 1835.

entries.card: notes:Braunhold's public-domain Andreas 1884 Sauganash engraving shows this attached log cabin with one doorway between two tall sash, their heads approximately on the doorway's head line. The identity is the existing the Illinois History Journal's Beaubien caption caption ruling in this record, not a new independent witness. These centres preserve the archetype's former symmetric stations on the attested 6.096 m frontage (centre 3.048 m, flanks at centre plus or minus 28 percent of the frontage), rounded to millimetres. Stating the set-out lets the existing archetype align the tall sash heads with the retained 1.95 m door head; no historical door or window station is claimed.

We used to guess one chimney only because it needed heat in winter. Now the picture shows it. That it comes up through the roof is from the picture. Its exact place and size are our guess. entries.card: notes:Built 'for the killing of such cattle as were required by the garrison at Fort Dearborn' (scan p. 1149) and working as a commercial packing house from 1833, when Clybourne 'packed some two hundred and fifty head of cattle and about two thousand hogs' and George W. Dole packed a further 250 cattle and 1,000 hogs at the same place; Andreas gives the prices, $2.80 a head average for the cattle and $3 per hundred pounds net for the hogs (scan p. 1151). THIS IS THE FIRST SLAUGHTER-HOUSE IN CHICAGO and the head of the trade that the city was later built on. Andreas elsewhere calls Archibald Clybourne 'the Government butcher for the Pottawatomies' (scan p. 253), a treaty-provision post — recorded here because it is what the man was, and flagged for review with the rest of this record's Indigenous content rather than paraphrased away.

levels.8-10: It was built to kill cattle for the soldiers at the fort. From 1833 it packed meat to sell. That year the owner packed about 250 cattle and 2,000 hogs. A man named Dole packed 250 cattle and 1,000 hogs here too. The book gives the prices. This was the first butcher house in Chicago. The city later grew big on this trade. The book also calls the owner the government's butcher for the Potawatomi. A treaty set up that job. That is what the man was, so we keep it. We mark it to be checked, like the rest of this record's Native history.

entries.card: notes:Built 1833 by James Kinzie — 'the first structure ever erected in the place for hotel purposes' — and standing at the north-east corner of Lake and Canal until it was moved in 1880 to 35 and 37 Milwaukee Avenue to clear the site for the Jones & Laughlin works. Both ends are attested, which is why a forty-seven-year span is tagged documented rather than being a research gap in disguise. IT IS STILL TOO LONG TO BE ONE FORM-STATE, and that is a known limitation: John Gray, landlord 1838-41, recalls 'a low one-story addition to the right, the same as on the left', so the building demonstrably grew, and nothing dates those additions. The phase should be split the moment they can be dated. A second, smaller conflict: chicagology's Green Tree page dates the move to 1880, while its Town of Chicago page, written in 1883, says the building was 'removed two years ago', i.e. 1881. Immaterial to the 1835 scene. The carpenter is disputed too — chicagology names 'Philo Cobb', DRLOIH names Silas B. Cobb, who is the historically real person and is almost certainly correct.

levels.8-10: Built in 1833 by James Kinzie, the first building in town made to be an inn. It stood at the corner of Lake and Canal until 1880. Then it was moved to Milwaukee Avenue, to make room for a big iron works. Both dates are known. But the building grew in that time. John Gray ran it from 1838 to 1841. He remembered a low one-floor room added on the right, the same as on the left. No one dates those rooms. Two pages of one website give 1880 and 1881 for the move. That does not matter for 1835. Who built it is mixed up too. One page says Philo Cobb. A book says Silas Cobb, a real man, and is almost for sure right.

entries.card: notes:CATON'S ATTIC IS THE POINT. It is the only account in this corpus of what an educated newcomer actually did for money and where he slept in the town's first summer, and it makes this building a lodging as well as an office - which is exactly the mixed use the reconstruction schedule's C-family roofs are for.

entries.card: notes:CORRECTED 2026-08-10 FROM 'crib', WITH ITS RE-BAKE. This record picked a disagreement and picked it wrong, and the source that settles it was signed by the eyewitness the losing argument leaned on. The 1883 old-settlers statement printed at Andreas pp. 631-632 — Caton, Bates, CLEAVER and Noble — says 'both bridges were built on abutments and two "bents"', and describes them: 'The bents were of four heavy logs, resting on the bottom, in deeper water.' So 'Bent' in the Kinzie Street page's chronology table is not a modern type-word applied down a column, as the superseded reasoning assumed; it is very probably that table reading this footnote, and it is the settlers' own word. WHAT THE MESH CAN AND CANNOT SHOW OF IT: the archetype now builds four heavy logs under a cap at each support, which is the count and the heaviness the sentence gives. 'Resting on the bottom' is the other half of it and is invisible here — this project models neither the riverbed nor anything more than half a metre below the waterline, so a bent stood on the bed and a bent driven into it are the same picture above water. The distinction lives in this note. THE SUPERSEDED REASONING, kept because it is what an honest reading of the thinner evidence looked like: A DISAGREEMENT PICKED WITH REASONING RATHER THAN SILENTLY. Cleaver describes heavy logs standing in shallow water, which is a crib — a log box, sunk and filled. The Kinzie Street page's chronology table instead types the bridge 'Wood, Fixed, Bent', and a bent is framed and usually pile-borne. Crib is adopted because Cleaver is an eyewitness describing what he saw and the table is a modern editorial classification applied uniformly down a column covering six bridges and a century. THE INFERENCE IS THE STEP FROM ABUTMENTS TO PIERS, not the choice between the two words: Cleaver describes the ends, nobody describes the middle, and this record assumes the intermediate supports were built the way the ends were. That last sentence is the one the footnote overturned: somebody did describe the middle.

entries.card: notes:FOUR IS THE ARCHETYPE'S NUMBER; WHAT THE SOURCE GIVES IS THE LOAD. The 1883 statement calls both branch bridges WAGON bridges with stringers of heavy logs running abutment to bent and bent to bent, and the 18 August 1835 procession crossed this one. A deck carrying teams over three spans of 18.7 m needs more than the two stringers of a footway, so four under a full-width deck is the load-carrying reading — but the number itself is nobody's, and a source that said three or five would replace it without disturbing anything else on this record. The North Branch record reaches the same value by a harder route, because that crossing is described as a footway in 1833 and has to be argued forward to 1835; this one is described as a wagon bridge from the start.

levels.8-10: Four is our number. What the record gives is the load. The 1883 paper calls both river bridges wagon bridges, with long heavy logs from end to bent and bent to bent. The parade of 18 August 1835 crossed this one. A deck carrying wagons over three spans of 18.7 meters needs more than the two logs of a footbridge. So four under a full deck is the strong reading. But the number is no one's. A record that said three or five would take its place, and change nothing else here. This one was called a wagon bridge from the start.

entries.card: notes:FOUR ROOMS AND A KITCHEN ARE ATTESTED; NO DIMENSION IS. Read as the commonest way four rooms were got under one roof in a frame house of 1834: a 24 x 18 ft story-and-a-half front range, two rooms on the ground floor and two chambers in the half-storey, with the kitchen as a 12 x 14 ft rear ell. 'With a kitchen ... attached to it' is read as an ell rather than a detached cook-house because the advertisement lists the barn and the garden in the same breath and they were plainly separate; a detached kitchen is the other honest reading and would change the plan, not the count. The whole is 24 x 32 ft, inside the D6 band (20x26-24x34 ft). Every number is invented.

A front part of 24 by 18 feet with a floor and a half: two rooms below, and two bedrooms under the roof. The kitchen is a 12 by 14 foot wing at the back. The ad says with a kitchen attached. We read it as a wing, not a cook house on its own. The ad names the barn and garden in the same line, and those were clearly apart. A kitchen on its own is the other fair reading. It would change the plan, not the count. The whole is 24 by 32 feet, inside our sizes.

It does not mean this crossing was finer than the town's main bridges. It is one wagon and one path wide, as asked.

entries.card: notes:Frame is attested; the framing METHOD is not. Balloon framing was developed in Chicago in 1832-33 and had become the dominant local method by the time this building went up, which makes it the better reading for 1834 — the opposite conclusion from the Sauganash of 1831, where the same reasoning argues for a braced frame. The distinction changes stud rhythm behind the sheathing and is not visible at this level of detail; it is recorded so the dataset's two frame taverns do not silently carry the same value for different reasons.

levels.8-10: Frame is known. The kind of frame is not. The light kind was first used in Chicago in 1832 and 1833. By the time this building went up, it was the usual one here. So it is the better guess for 1834. That is the opposite of the Sauganash of 1831, where the same reason gives the older kind. It cannot be seen from outside. We record it so our two frame inns do not quietly get the same answer for different reasons.

entries.card: notes:Gable is inferred from the frame building's typology and the undated Moss engraving. The previous statement that the absence of a steeple was attested specifically for 1835 is superseded: the text dates that absence to construction in 1833, and the present belfry is a declared reconstruction within the unresolved addition interval. The original gabled type, footprint and wall height are retained; its pitch is a separate reconstructed picture-bounded choice.

The roof's shape, the building's size and its wall height stay the same.

levels.8-10: Long outer braces, a test. The 1884 picture shows long braces on the outside, fixed high on the tall posts. Before, ours were fixed only 2.6 meters above the bridge floor. Now they are fixed at 5.2 meters, below the top of the frame. That tests what the picture shows. The other sizes are our guess, not measured.

entries.card: notes:HORIZONTAL-BOARD PARAPETS. The public-domain plate published in Andreas in 1884, page 631, draws broad side parapets with horizontal joints along the approaches and closed draw. This is retrospective pictorial form, inferred for the 1835 bridge rather than a contemporary specification, coordinate, footprint dimension or surveyed height. Retain the existing 0.95 m overall parapet height and approximately 2.2 m post bays; five 162 mm courses, 40 mm thickness, 10 mm gaps, 40 mm lower clearance and 200 by 60 mm cap are reconstructed scantlings. Panels and caps stop at post bays, draw ends and the existing two-leaf meeting line. Post heads end at 0.89 m under the cap. The old pole-rail description records the prior default detail. The flat deck, original cribs and every existing height/placement control remain unchanged; the central rise, approaches, mechanism and camera remain unresolved. No accepted match is claimed.

levels.8-10: Side walls of boards laid flat. A picture printed in a book in 1884 shows wide side walls with flat boards along the bridge. That picture was drawn later, so using it for 1835 is a guess. The height of the side wall stays at 0.95 meters, with posts about 2.2 meters apart. The sizes of the boards and caps are our guess. Nothing else on the bridge changes. We do not claim a match.

entries.card: notes:HOW TALL THE GALLOWS STOOD IS THE MOST VISIBLE UNKNOWN IN THIS DATASET. No source gives the height, the section, the bracing or the tackle of these frames; what survives is that they were tall enough to be frightening at night and strong enough to hold a sixty-foot draw suspended for forty-eight hours. 6.4 m above the deck — about twenty-one feet — is the archetype's own number, chosen so that a frame is unmistakably a gallows against the sky and not a gatepost, and it is not a finding. THE REASON IT IS BUILT AT ALL, rather than declared absent: the confidence view exists exactly for this. A dithered translucent frame says 'this shape is ours' in a way no footnote can, and leaving the frames out would tell a visitor the town's one piece of engineering was a plain causeway, which is a stronger false claim than a tagged guess. The alternative reading was on this record for a few hours on 2026-08-11 and is recorded here because it is a real argument: build nothing, declare it, and let the liberties document carry the frames in prose. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: the February 1834 proposals Andreas mentions, the trustees' specification, the twenty-five-dollar premium drawing, or any period view of the river mouth looking west.

levels.8-10: How tall the tall frames over the bridge stood is the biggest thing we can see but do not know. No record gives their height, shape or ropes. We know they were tall enough to look scary at night, and strong enough to hold the sixty-foot bridge part up for two days. 6.4 meters, about 21 feet, is our usual number. It makes a frame look like a lifting frame, not a gate post. It is not a finding. We build them anyway, see-through in the confidence view, to say this shape is ours. Leaving them out would say the bridge was just a plain road over the water, and that would be more wrong. Plans from 1834, or any old picture of the river mouth, could settle it.

entries.card: notes:HUBBARD SAYS TWO STOREYS OF THE FACTOR HOUSE; THIS RECORD SAYS THEY ARE BLOCK A'S, AND THAT SECOND STEP IS THE INFERENCE. The prose names one building — 'the "Factor House", a two-story, squared-log structure' — and the plate letters that name against three blocks, so which of the three carries the storeys is not on the sheet. A is taken to be it on two grounds stated rather than assumed: the label's first letter stands about 2 m clear of A's north-east end and touches no other block, and A at 20.4 x 7.9 m is the only one of the three a two-storey dwelling-and-store will fit (B is a 16.6 x 5.1 m bar set across it, C is 6.7 x 5.0 m). Neither ground is proof and the grade is `inferred` because of it. THE ALTERNATIVE THE TICKET ALLOWED — 'not determinable, so the storey count is inferred from the type' — would have put ONE storey here on no evidence at all while a witness was sitting on the shelf saying two; taking the witness and writing down exactly how far it had to be carried is the better of the two answers, and this note is that distance.

levels.8-10: Hubbard says the trading house had two floors. We say the two floors are block A's, and that is our guess. Hubbard names one building, a two-floor house of squared logs. The plan writes that name over three blocks. So which block it is, is not on the map. We pick A for two reasons. The label starts just past A's corner and touches no other block. And A is the only one big enough for a home and store with two floors. Neither reason is proof. The other way would have put one floor here on no proof at all, while a man who saw it said two. Taking his word, and saying how far we had to carry it, is the better answer.

entries.card: notes:HUBBARD'S ADJECTIVE IS THE WHOLE OF THE EVIDENCE AND IT IS NOT A MATERIAL. He calls them 'rude wash-houses', which says rough and says nothing about what they were rough in. Plank — sawn boards nailed up vertically with the gaps showing — is the archetype's reading of a rough working building put up quickly for a wet trade, and it is preferred to log here for one stated reason: a laundry wants air and light through its walls and a notched log pen gives neither. The reasoning is the inference; nobody wrote it down.

levels.8-10: Hubbard's one word is all we have, and it does not say what it was made of. He calls them rough wash houses. That says rough, but not rough in what. We build it of boards nailed up and down, with gaps between. That is our idea of a rough work building put up fast for wet work. We pick it over logs for one reason. A wash house wants air and light through its walls, and a log building gives neither. That is our reason. No one wrote it down.

levels.8-10: Hubbard says in 1827 that the fort's leaders lived in it. A list from 1855 calls it the leader's house. A book says the officers had rooms inside the fort's walls.

entries.card: notes:Hubbard calls it 'the military barn' and the 1830 plan draws the Big Barn with Cupola inside the fort's own fenced ground, beside the Cultivated Field belonging to The Fort. The post was garrisoned continuously from June 1832 to 29 December 1836 (the stockade's own occupants block, after Andreas), so on 1 July 1835 its service buildings were the garrison's; the people are seated on the stockade and are not repeated here.

entries.card: notes:Hubbard calls it 'the military barn' in so many words; the plan calls it the Big Barn with Cupola and draws it inside the fort's fenced ground beside the Cultivated Field belonging to The Fort. What was kept in it is not stated and is not inferred here: a barn on a post of this date held forage, teams and the field's implements, but which of those is a guess and the record claims the building, not its contents.

What was kept in it is not known, and we do not guess. A fort's barn held hay, horses and farm tools, but which of those is a guess. The record claims the building, not what was in it.

entries.card: notes:Hubbard names 'the sutler's store' in 1827 and the 1855 photograph key letters 'D is the Sutler's'. AN ALTERNATIVE IDENTIFICATION EXISTS AND IS NOT RESOLVED: Robert Fergus, describing the fort in 1850, mentions 'another building in the Fort enclosure ... just east of the block-house' which 'was the quartermaster's or sutler's quarters' - his own 'or'. That building is at the other end of the fort from this one, so it is either a second building this project does not model or a confused memory; either way no quartermaster's quarters is built, because a source that cannot decide between two names is not evidence for either.

So it is a second building we do not build, or a mixed-up memory. We build no quartermaster's rooms. A record that cannot pick between two names is not proof of either.

entries.card: notes:Hubbard: 'the magazine, of brick'. One of only two brick buildings in the fort. GUARD ON A TEMPTING PARALLEL: the 1803 War Department instruction for this class of post specified 'the magazines for powder to be of brick of a conic figure', which is quoted in the same literature - but that is the specification for the FIRST fort, and it is not evidence that this magazine was conical. It is built as a plain gabled block.

entries.card: notes:INVENTED WITHIN A DOCUMENTED SIDE. Fergus puts the artillery house on the east of the parade with the barracks and the storehouse; the 1830 plan draws only one range on that side and this project reads that range as the barracks, because Hubbard's 1827 sentence fixes the barracks there and the sutler's north of it. So there is no drawn building for this record to sit on. It is placed inside the east curtain at the south end - the one part of that side the plan leaves empty - clear of the barracks by about a metre and of the south wall by about three. Every one of those numbers is ours.

entries.card: notes:INVENTED, AND THE ARITHMETIC BEHIND IT IS STATED SO IT CAN BE ARGUED WITH. No source reached gives this building a dimension. What IS documented is its cost, about $900, and its storey count, two - and this dataset now holds two contemporary buildings whose cost AND area are both attested: the First Presbyterian Church at $600 for 1,000 sq ft ($0.60/sq ft) and St Mary's at $400 for 875 sq ft ($0.46/sq ft). Two storeys at the midpoint of that range, about $0.55 per square foot, buys roughly 1,600 sq ft of floor, i.e. about 800 sq ft per storey. 30 x 25 ft is 750 sq ft, which at $0.55 gives $825 against the attested $900 - close, and on the conservative side. 9.144 x 7.62 m is 30 x 25 ft, recorded converted with the original figures stated. THIS IS STILL AN INVENTION AND IT IS TAGGED AS ONE. The cost-per-square-foot of a two-storey building is not the cost-per-square-foot of a single-storey one (a second floor is cheap relative to a roof and a foundation, which would make the real building BIGGER than this), and both reference figures rest on the citation problem set out in the Presbyterian record's research note. The 25 ft depth is additionally borrowed - it is the depth of both churches and of the rectangle four other records in this dataset use - so the shape is a claim about the type and not about this building.

entries.card: notes:MARCH 1832, AND THE YEAR THIS RECORD CITED ANDREAS FOR IS NOT A YEAR ANDREAS GIVES. Until 2026-08-16 the range opened at 1833-03-01, under a note reading 'MARCH 1833 IS ATTESTED AS A MONTH AND CONTESTED AS A YEAR ... The dossier notes that some accounts give 1832 instead'. Andreas gives 1832 in both places he treats the pen, and 1833 in neither. The narrative: 'The result of this generosity on the part of the State was seen in March, 1832, when, through the architectural skill of Samuel Miller, contractor, there arose upon the southwest corner of the square, the so-called "estray-pen." Although sometimes designated and dignified as "the first public building ever erected in Chicago," the "pen" was a small wooden enclosure and quite roofless' (Andreas I scan p. 365). The chronological index: the entry 'First public building (the "Estray Pen") erected' stands under the heading 1832, between '1832 - (January) - First Methodist quarterly meeting' and '(April) - First street leading to the lake laid out' (scan p. 1315). The month was read off that index correctly and the year off the wrong heading. NOTHING IN THE SCENE MOVES. The pen stands on 1835-07-01 under either reading and is roofless under both - which is why it is worth saying that the correction is to the CITATION and not to the town: a note that cites a source for a value the source does not carry is wrong in the way this project cares most about, whether or not anything visible depends on it. THE RANGE IS NOW WIDE, AND HONESTLY SO: 1832-03-01 is the first day of the attested month in the attested year, and 1835-12-31 remains A HOUSEKEEPING BOUND, NOT A REMOVAL DATE. Nothing reached says when the pen came down. What IS attested is that its role as a place of confinement ended in the fall of 1833 when the log jail went up at the other corner of the same block - which is a change of use, not of fabric, and does not close the phase. ROADMAP T-I3.

levels.8-10: March 1832. Our record used to say 1833 and cite a book for it, but the book never gives 1833. It gives 1832 both times it tells of the pen. It says that in March 1832, Samuel Miller built the so-called stray pen on the corner of the square. People called it the first public building in Chicago. It was a small wooden fence with no roof. The book's list of dates puts it under 1832 too. We read the month right but the year from the wrong line. Nothing in the scene changes. The pen stands in July 1835, with no roof, either way. The pen stopped holding prisoners in the fall of 1833, when the log jail went up nearby.

entries.card: notes:MEASURED, AND LARGER THAN A BLOCKHOUSE OUGHT TO BE. 14.52 x 9.80 m is about 48 x 32 ft, read off the 1830 plan at the derived scale after correcting for the fort's rotation. A period blockhouse is usually 20 to 30 ft square, so this is either an unusually large one or - more likely - the plate drawing the blockhouse together with the return of the curtain round it as a single heavy block. The measurement is recorded rather than quietly shrunk to the expected size, because shrinking it would be substituting a typology for the only plan that exists. Carry +/-25 percent and read the note.

entries.card: notes:NEITHER END IS DATED BY A SOURCE and both are the honest bounds of what is attested. THE START is McKee's own arrival: Andreas has him engaged as the agency blacksmith the 1821 treaty required and reaching Fort Dearborn in June 1823, finding 'but two houses on the north side of the river' and building the fourth himself. 1823 is the first year he can have kept a house here and it is the year the neighbouring shop record opens on for the same reason. THE END IS THE HONEST MINIMUM, and it is the weakest line on this record: Andreas's vicinity list describes the settlement about 1830 and Wau-Bun the ring in 1831, and after that nothing names this building. The argument for 1835 is the argument the shop record makes — a Government smith was still owed to the Potawatomi under the 1821 and 1833 treaties — and it is an argument about an obligation rather than about a house. Tagged inferred for that reason.

He reached Fort Dearborn in June 1823, and found only two houses on the north side of the river. He built the fourth himself. 1823 is the first year he could have kept a house here. The case for 1835 is that the Potawatomi were still owed a blacksmith by the treaties of 1821 and 1833. That is about a promise, not a house. So it is marked as our guess.

entries.card: notes:NEITHER END IS DATED BY A SOURCE. THE START is the light itself: Samuel Jackson completed the second tower in 1832, and the keepership Andreas records — Samuel Lasby, the first keeper, 'at $350 a year with quarters' — is an office that exists from the night the light was first kept. A station's quarters are not later than its light. THE END is the scene's own window and not a statement about the building: nothing reached says when these quarters were replaced, and the 1835-12-31 bound is the honest limit of what this project's corpus covers rather than a fate. Both ends are inferred for those reasons.

entries.card: notes:NO SOURCE DATES THIS BUILDING AT EITHER END; both dates are the honest bounds of what is attested. THE START: Andreas says only 'After the second Fort Dearborn was built, David McKee was appointed Government blacksmith, his shop being situated near the Agency House, at the foot of State Street' — the fort was rebuilt in 1816 — but the same book fixes McKee's arrival: he was engaged as the agency blacksmith the 1821 treaty required and, by his own recollection, reached Fort Dearborn in June 1823, finding 'but two houses on the north side of the river' and building the fourth himself. 1823 is therefore the first year the shop can have stood under him, and the range opens there rather than at 1816. THE END IS THE HONEST MINIMUM. The shop is attested standing around 1830 — 'In its vicinity were small log buildings occupied by the blacksmith, Mr. McKee, and Billy Caldwell' — and in 1831 Wau-Bun still describes the ring of agency log residences with a blacksmith among them. After that nothing. McKee himself had other work by then; he was carrying the Government mail to Fort Wayne monthly from 1827-28 and later farmed on the Des Plaines. A GOVERNMENT SMITH WAS STILL OWED TO THE POTAWATOMI IN 1835 under the 1821 and 1833 treaties, which is the argument for the shop still standing on the scene date, and it is an argument about an obligation rather than about a building. Tagged inferred for that reason.

levels.8-10: No record dates this building at either end. Andreas says David McKee was the government's blacksmith, with a shop near the Agency House. McKee came here in June 1823, so that is the first year the shop could stand. Records show the shop around 1830 and 1831. After that, nothing. McKee had other work by then. entries.card: notes:NOBODY DESCRIBED THE MIDDLE OF THIS BRIDGE AND ZERO IS THE ANSWER THAT INVENTS LEAST. The archetype accepts 0 explicitly — 'a short crossing lands abutment to abutment with nothing in the water' — and without a stated count it would fall back to a spacing of 4.5 m and put a support in the middle of an 8 m span. An 8 m run of log stringers needs no intermediate bent; the branch bridges needed two each over 56 and 72 m. So the count is inference from the span, and it keeps a pier out of a stream nobody says had one.

entries.card: notes:NOT AN INN AT THE SCENE DATE, and that is the most important fact this record carries. Miller's tavern competed with the Wolf Point Tavern from 1830, but Wau-Bun, describing 1831, already calls the Miller house 'at this time vacant', Miller having removed to the place that was becoming Michigan City; DRLOIH has the business converted to a store run by P. F. W. Peck after 1832; and a third account has Miller retiring from the field in 1834. The three disagree in their chronology and agree in their direction. Modelled as present and in secondary store or residential use, not innkeeping. The specific claim that Peck was running it does not survive to the scene date either — this project's own exclusions record places Peck in 1835 at his two-storey frame store at South Water and LaSalle.

levels.8-10: Not an inn on the day we show. That is the most important fact here. Miller's inn competed with the Wolf Point inn from 1830. But Wau-Bun, telling of 1831, already calls the Miller house empty at this time. Miller had moved to what was becoming Michigan City. A book says it became a store, run by Peck, after 1832. Another says Miller left the trade in 1834. The three do not agree on dates, but all point the same way. So we show it standing, used as a store or home, not an inn. Peck running it does not last to 1835 either. Our own notes put Peck in 1835 at his store of two floors at South Water and LaSalle.

entries.card: notes:NOT AN OPERATING INDIAN AGENCY BUILDING AT THE SCENE DATE, most likely, and that is the fact this record has least evidence for. Andreas has it 'left unoccupied by the death of Dr. Wolcott' in 1830, then in the autumn of 1832 describes 'the old Indian agency-house in which Colonel Hamilton then resided' — Colonel R. J. Hamilton, the county's clerk and commissioner of school lands, living in it as a private house while the agency's business ran down through the 1833 treaty. Nothing reached says who was in it in July 1835 or what it was being used for, so the value records a residence and this record carries no occupants block rather than guessing at one.

entries.card: notes:NOT ATTESTED EITHER WAY, and the archetype reads it, so leaving it out would have chosen a finish silently. Unpainted weathered clapboard is the default reading for a frontier tavern's addition and it is weakly supported by the contrast Wau-Bun draws at Wolf Point in 1831, where a painted white building was 'the admiration of all the little circle' precisely because the buildings around it were not painted. Still a choice.

Nothing says he painted this one, and unpainted is the cheaper reading for a speculative-boom house. Still a choice.

entries.card: notes:NOT ATTESTED FOR THIS BUILDING BY ANY SOURCE REACHED, and the number is inference from use rather than from description. Calhoun secured an OFFICE in the building while a store traded from the same corner, so the building held at least two tenancies; a two-storey block is how that is normally arranged on a corner lot on this street, and Peck's store one block west is documented two-storey frame. A single storey is possible and would make the building a third smaller in elevation. DO NOT READ THE WOODCUT IN THE 26 NOVEMBER 1833 ISSUE AS EVIDENCE: the 'Two Buildings to Let' advertisement carries an engraving of a three-storey building with regular fenestration, and it is a printer's generic stock cut, not a picture of a Chicago building. Nothing in this record derives from it.

levels.8-10: No record says, so this is a guess from how it was used. The paper had an office here, and a store sold goods from the same corner. So at least two businesses shared it. entries.card: notes:NOTHING IN ANY SOURCE PLACES THIS WORKS. The advertisement names the firm and the trade and no street; Andreas's summary of the same columns names the firm and the trade and no street. So this coordinate is a proposal and is tagged conjectural, and it cites no sources because none supports it. THE REASONING, WHICH IS A PREFERENCE AND NOT EVIDENCE, IN TWO PARTS. First the DIVISION: Daniel Elston is a North Branch figure. Elston Avenue, the plank road that ran north-west along the branch, is named for him, and Andreas's street-naming chapter refers to 'the Elston road' as a fixed landmark (scan p. 409); his later brickyard, the largest in the city by 1854, worked clay on the same side of the town (scan p. 1169). None of that is 1833 and none of it is this building. Second the SITING: soap and candle making is rendering — boiling tallow with lye leached from wood ash — and it is one of the loudest-smelling trades there is. Nuisance trades sit at the edge of a town, downwind and on water, near the slaughtering that supplies the tallow; Archibald Clybourne's slaughter-house was on this same branch. That is an argument about how towns arrange themselves, and towns are not obliged to obey it. THE ALTERNATIVE READING IS AT LEAST AS GOOD: every other advertiser in that issue of the Democrat whose address is known was on or near South Water Street, and a manufactory that wanted the town's house ashes had a reason to be where the houses were. METHOD, such as it is: the works stand on the east bank of the North Branch about 190 m above the forks, 16 m back from the traced bank line, on modelled ground and clear of every other structure in the dataset. Facade bearing 270, due west onto the branch. TREAT THE WHOLE PLACEMENT AS A PROPOSAL, correctable by one line of an 1834 or 1835 advertisement.

NOTE THE CONSEQUENCE, WHICH IS A FEATURE OF THE CONVERSION AND NOT AN ERROR: a 2.3 m stable door cut into a 2.5 m cabin wall leaves only 0.2 m of header. That tightness is what converting a dwelling into a barn actually looks like — the wall was built for a person and the opening was cut for a horse — and it is why this record states the wall height rather than letting the archetype's size-aware default (2.71 m) quietly buy the door more room than the building had.

entries.card: notes:No source gives a storey count. One storey with a loft under the roof is the standard form for a log tavern of this date and region, and it is what the attested loft implies: Caton's court sat 'in the unfinished loft', which is a roof space and not a second storey. It is also the conservative reading - the sources that do describe height in this town single out the Sauganash's two storeys and Miller's two-storey frame range as remarkable, which they would not be if every tavern had two. Not attested either way.

entries.card: notes:Not attested for this building. entries.card: notes:ONE WITNESS, AND IT IS PRE-1835. The range opens 24 February 1830, the date on the Harrison plan, because that plan is the only source this project holds that says anything at all about this building — Hubbard describes the fort's well and its wash-houses and says nothing about out buildings, so the second witness the wash house record carries does not exist here. IT CLOSES 29 DECEMBER 1836, the evacuation, and that is a floor rather than a demolition: nothing attests when the fort's outer buildings came down. WHAT CARRIES THE SCENE DATE OF 1 JULY 1835 is the middle of that range and not either end of it — the post was garrisoned continuously from June 1832 to 29 December 1836, so a service building the garrison's own engineer drew in 1830 is standing five years later unless something says it stopped, and nothing does. That is an argument, not an assumption, and it is the argument every Fort Dearborn record here rests on. IT IS A THINNER ARGUMENT THAN THE WASH HOUSE'S because it stands on one witness instead of two, and the grade says so.

levels.8-10: One floor, partly built, is our choice for July 1835. It could have been anywhere from nothing to two floors. A notice of 10 June says work had started. Bonnell, years later, tells of it being built, but gives three different years. Martineau tells of it unfinished in June 1836. A book says it opened in the fall of 1836. So it was not done, but we cannot tell how far it was in July. We build one part done floor, with no roof and no hotel inside.

entries.card: notes:PICTURE-BOUNDED 1835 RECONSTRUCTION. Andreas p.290 states that the church had no tower when built in 1833 and received a low open tower and bell some time afterwards, without an installation date. The undated Moss engraving on p.291 shows an open belfry, curved pointed cap and cross. This model chooses that recognizable form for 1835 as a reconstruction, not proof of its presence by July 1835 or a dated interpretation of the engraving. The four posts, low crossed rails, curved braces, boarded plinth, small bell, cap and cross use chosen dimensions recorded in the liberty. No later enlargement, relocation or phase is adopted. Tower presence is a chosen temporal reconstruction, not a dated witness.

levels.8-10: Our guess for 1835, from a picture. A book says the church had no tower when it was built in 1833. Some time later it got a low open tower and a bell, but no date is given. Moss's print, with no date, shows an open bell tower, a curved pointed cap and a cross. We use that shape for 1835 as our guess. It does not prove the tower was there by July 1835. Its posts, rails, bell, cap and cross have sizes we chose. Tower or no tower in 1835 is our choice, not a dated record.

entries.card: notes:PLACED 2026-08-09. NO SURVIVING INTERSECTION LOCATES THIS BUILDING — the streets platted across this ground in Kinzie's Addition were staked in 1833-35 and the point itself has since been rebuilt — so the coordinate is derived from the datum origin at the forks confluence and from bank geometry. What is attested is unusually consistent for this dataset: chicagology, 'The Miller House stood on the point of land between the North Branch and the Main Channel'; Wau-Bun, 'on the north side of the river ... near the forks'; DRLOIH, a store 'on the north bank of the river at the forks'; and the Miller-Clybourn ferry ran across the North Branch between this house and the Wolf Point Tavern, which requires it to be on the point. A FOURTH SOURCE DISAGREES AND IS TREATED AS AN ERROR: the hotel chronology places Miller on the 'south branch of Chicago River, opposite Wolf Point'. Four independent statements against one, and the ferry route settles it. Method: modern water polygons from OpenStreetMap put the nose of the point at about 39 m north of the datum origin, with the main-stem north bank running east from there and the North Branch east bank running north-west. The footprint's south face is set 14 m north of the main-stem bank and its west face about 22 m east of the North Branch bank, which puts the building on the point and off both waters. Working uncertainty about 20 m from the georeference, plus an unquantified allowance for the modern banks not being the 1835 banks — this ground was filled and wharfed and is now built over, and unlike the west bank there is no street line here to check it against, so treat the along-bank position as the softer of the two axes. Facade bearing 180, due south onto the main stem, from 'a two-story house ... fronting the river'. On a point the river is on two sides: a bearing of about 215, fronting the confluence and Wolf Point across the water, is equally arguable and would rotate the building about 35 degrees. Local-origin normalization for the reconstructed adjacent compound translates the origin(-6,+5)m in the retained180-degree footprint frame, equivalent to UTM(+6,-5)m. This keeps the tall range's wall box and six front opening world positions unchanged while moving the low core beside it; it does not add a surveyed location. The old20 m placement uncertainty and facade bearing remain. Roof-joint vertices and fractional flue station are governed by the end-route limits, not a whole-mesh equality claim.

levels.8-10: No street corner left today shows where this building stood. The streets here were laid out in 1833 to 1835, and the point has been built over since. So its place is worked out from where the rivers meet and the shape of the banks. What is known agrees well. One page says the Miller House stood on the point of land between the North Branch and the main river. Wau-Bun says on the north side of the river, near the forks. A book says a store on the north bank at the forks. And the Miller ferry ran across the North Branch between this house and the Wolf Point inn, which puts it on the point. One record puts Miller on the south branch, across from Wolf Point. We treat that as a mistake. It is four against one, and the ferry settles it. We used today's river maps to find the point, and set the house back from both rivers. It could be off by about 20 meters, more along the bank, since the banks have been filled and built over. The front faces south onto the river, from a house facing the river. On a point, the river is on two sides, so it could face the forks instead.

entries.card: notes:PLACED 2026-08-09. The corner is documented — chicagology and the Chicago Landmark record both put the Sauganash at the south-east corner of Lake and Market — but the COORDINATE is inferred, so the tag follows the weaker half. Method: Market Street is today's N Wacker Drive and Lake Street is unchanged, an equivalence the research dossier states and the georeference independently corroborates, since the 1834 plats warped onto the modern street centrelines at 17.5 m RMS. The modern intersection centre was read from OpenStreetMap (EPSG:26916 E 447161.9, N 4637285.4) and the footprint origin offset 12.2 m east and 20.2 m south of it: half of an 80 ft platted street to reach the kerb, and the footprint's own 8 m depth so the building's north face sits on the Lake Street frontage of a south-east corner lot. Working uncertainty about 20 m, which is the georeference's, not an additional guess. Facade bearing 0 (north, onto Lake Street): the sources say it faced the forks to the north-west, so the true bearing is likely nearer 315, but the plat lot lines are orthogonal and a corner building fronting Lake is the defensible reading until better evidence appears.

levels.8-10: Placed on 9 August 2026. The corner is known. A website and the city's landmark record both put the Sauganash at the south-east corner of Lake and Market. But the exact spot is our guess, so the grade follows the weaker half. Market Street is today's Wacker Drive, and Lake Street is the same. The old maps fit today's streets well. We found the corner on today's maps, and set the building just inside the south-east corner lot, facing Lake Street. It could be off by about 20 meters. The front faces north, onto Lake Street. The records say it faced the forks to the north-west, so it may have turned more that way. But the lots are square to the streets, so a corner building facing Lake is the safer reading.

entries.card: notes:PLACED 2026-08-11, AND ONE BOOK CONTRADICTS ITSELF ABOUT WHICH SIDE OF CLARK STREET IT WAS ON. The schools chapter says twice that the building stood 'on the north bank of the river, just east of Clark Street' and 'on the river bank just east of Clark Street'. The Methodist chapter says 'the Watkins school-house, which was located on North Water Street, between Clark and LaSalle' — which is WEST of Clark, about a block away. THE SCHOOLS CHAPTER IS ADOPTED because it is the more specific statement, it is made twice, and it is the chapter about this building; the church chapter is naming a meeting place in passing. IF THE CHURCH CHAPTER IS RIGHT, THIS BUILDING STANDS ABOUT 110 M WEST OF WHERE IT IS DRAWN. Method: Clark Street's modern centreline was read from OpenStreetMap through the Kinzie intersection (EPSG:26916 E 447646.20, N 4637668.88, local E +573.5, N +273.1) and carried south on the OSM bearing, giving an east kerb 12.2 m east of it, half an 80 ft platted street; the 1834 north bank and the North Water Street frontage were read off the Wright 1834 sheet through this project's fitted affine, which puts the drawn bank at local N +98 along this stretch and the block row's south line — the street's north kerb — at about N +128. The building is set with its west face 6 m east of the Clark kerb and its south face 12.5 m north of the bank, i.e. on the bank strip the street occupies, which is what 'on the river bank' says. Facade bearing 180, due south to the river, is inferred from that frontage and from nothing anybody wrote. UNCERTAINTY: about 20 m from the georeference, plus the ~5 m of reading the sheet by eye, plus the block-scale disagreement above, which is far larger than either. There is no modelled terrain under this building — it stands about 280 m east of the terrain box.

entries.card: notes:PLACED BY A SENTENCE, NOT BY THE PLAN. The 1830 plan draws no magazine; the only positional evidence is Hubbard in 1827: 'the magazine, of brick, was situated about half way between the west end of the guard and block-houses.' That reading is what put the guard house on the WEST side of the south gate rather than the east - it is the only assignment of the two flanking buildings that leaves a real gap for the magazine to stand in - and this position is the midpoint of that gap, just inside the curtain in the south-west quarter of the enclosure. UNCERTAINTY IS LARGER THAN THE REST OF THE COMPLEX: 'about half way' is the whole of it, and the sentence can be parsed two ways (midway between the two buildings' west ends, or midway between the guard house's west end and the block-house), which move the point about 4 m apart. The rotation is the fort's.

entries.card: notes:PLACED FROM THE PLAN AND CORROBORATED BY TWO TEXTS. The 1830 plan draws a heavy hollow block at the south-west angle, projecting outside the curtain on both faces - the only element of the fort drawn that way. Andreas: 'The block-house was in the southwest corner.' Hubbard, 1827: 'the block-house was located at the southwest and the bastion at the northwest corners of the fort.' Three sources, one corner. The rotation is the fort's.

entries.card: notes:PLACEHOLDER - NO DIMENSION IS ATTESTED, BUT THE SIZE IS BOUNDED TWICE AND THE TWO BOUNDS PULL AGAINST EACH OTHER. Bonnell calls it "a small yellow house" and then says Mrs. Kelsey "had all the boarders that she could accommodate" and turned him away. So: small enough to be called small, and full enough to refuse a lodger. 8.5 x 6.1 m is about 28 x 20 ft - a hall-and-parlour front range with chambers in the half storey, which is where boarders slept. Every number is invented; what is not invented is that this is the smallest of the two houses this parcel raises, because one source calls it small and the other calls its neighbour a residence.

levels.8-10: No size is known, but two clues pull against each other. Bonnell calls it a small yellow house. Then he says Mrs. Kelsey had all the boarders she could take, and turned him away. So it was small, but full. 8.5 by 6.1 meters is about 28 by 20 feet. It has two front rooms, and rooms under the roof where boarders slept. Every number is our guess. What is not a guess is that it is the smaller of the two houses here. One record calls it small, and calls the other a home.

entries.card: notes:PLACEHOLDER - NO DIMENSION IS ATTESTED. 11.0 x 8.0 m is about 36 x 26 ft, an eaves-front house of two rooms and a passage on the front range. Every number is invented. The only thing bounding the size is who lived here: Bonnell calls it a "residence" rather than a house or a cabin, and its occupant is a physician and half of a South Water Street drug firm, so the house is given the frontage of a professional man's dwelling and not a labourer's cabin. That is an argument about a trade and not a measurement. It is deliberately smaller than the frame houses this project has raised on stated dimensions, because nothing here is stated at all.

entries.card: notes:PLACEHOLDER — NO DIMENSION IS ATTESTED, but unlike most of the invented footprints in this dataset this one has a CAPACITY behind it and the size was chosen against that capacity rather than freely. Andreas records 250 head of cattle and about 2,000 hogs packed here by Clybourne in 1833, plus 250 head of cattle and 1,000 hogs packed at the same place by George W. Dole (scan p. 1151) — a season's throughput on that scale needs a killing floor several beasts wide, hanging room, and a working yard beside it. 12 x 9 m is about 39 x 30 ft, which is a large log building by the standards of this town and a small one by the standards of that throughput; the 12 m runs along the bank and the 9 m is the depth. Every number is invented and the polygon cites no sources. WHAT IS NOT MODELLED IS ARGUABLY THE BIGGER HALF: the killing pens, the stock yard that later gave the trade the Bull's Head name, and the packing gear are all outside this footprint and outside this archetype, which builds a building and not a works. To resolve: Andreas vol. 1 at page-image level around scan pp. 1149-1151, or any Cook County or Fort Dearborn contract paper describing the premises.

entries.card: notes:PLACEHOLDER — NO DIMENSIONS ARE ATTESTED. Only two adjectives are, and THEY CONFLICT: Wau-Bun calls it 'a small square log building', chicagology calls it 'an oblong building'. Square is adopted for the proportion because Wau-Bun is the earlier and nearer-primary witness and was describing what she saw, while chicagology's is a recollection transcribed at further remove — but a 7 x 7 m square is a guess at scale wearing an attested proportion, so the whole polygon is tagged conjectural and cites no sources. 7 m is about 23 ft, a single-pen log building large enough for ten founding members and a school. entries.card: notes:PREVIOUS CRIB-ONLY RECONSTRUCTION, retained as history: NOBODY SAID. The branch bridges' supports are documented as bents of four heavy logs resting on the bottom, because four men who used them wrote it down; nothing equivalent exists for this crossing, and the sentence that would have settled it is the one Andreas did not write. Crib is chosen over the archetype's other two readings — bent and pile — on the ground that it is the archetype's own default and that the harbour works at the mouth of the same river were at that moment being built of timber cribs by federal engineers, in a town whose one shipwright had just framed this bridge. That is a reason to prefer it and not evidence for it, so the tag is conjectural rather than inferred, and the count beside it carries the same chip for the same reason. CURRENT PICTURE-BOUNDED RECONSTRUCTION: the retrospective Andreas plate distinguishes broad draw-bearing foundations from the lighter trestle-like approach supports. Use the existing four-log bent for the remaining approach stations; that count, section and riverbed seating are reconstructed, not evidence that the Dearborn crossing used the branch bridges' documented construction. The two selected frame bearings override this general kind with separately dimensioned reconstructed crib platforms. No source coordinate, surveyed foundation footprint or accepted whole-picture match follows. CURRENT PLATFORM CORRECTION: the two selected bearings now use boarded pile-supported caps rather than the rejected V3 solid-crib trial; all numerical sections and counts remain reconstructed.

levels.8-10: No one wrote down what held the bridge up. The branch bridges stood on frames of four heavy logs, because four men who used them said so. Nothing like that exists for this bridge. We first chose boxes of logs filled with stone, our usual kind. The harbor works nearby were being built that way then. That is a reason, not a proof. Now an old picture from 1884 shows big wide bases under the lifting part, and lighter frames under the rest. So the rest stand on four-log frames, our guess. The two big bases are built on their own.

entries.card: notes:READ FROM A DRAWING CONVENTION, NOT FROM A CAPTION. The 1830 plate draws two sides of this plot as a continuous zigzag line and the other two as plain lines. entries.card: notes:RENTAL HOUSING STOCK, OTHERWISE INVISIBLE. entries.card: notes:SAWN PLANK RATHER THAN RIVEN PUNCHEON, AND IT IS THE FIRST RECORD IN THIS DATASET TO CARRY THE VALUE. The branch bridges' floor is documented as 'puncheons or split logs', which is what a crew lays without a sawyer. This bridge was different in the one way that decides the question: Norton 'commenced cutting the lumber' in the winter of 1833-34 and spent three months building from it, to a design that had won a premium, on a structure with a moving leaf. Riven stock of uneven width is not what a ship-carpenter frames a hoisted draw and its approaches from. The mesh differs accordingly — narrower boards, laid regularly, with the ends in line instead of the ragged butts a split floor gives. THE INFERENCE IS FROM THE BUILDER AND THE MATERIAL WORD, not from any statement about the deck, and 'cutting the lumber' could in principle describe felling rather than sawing. It is graded inferred for that reason.

So the boards are narrow and even. But cutting the lumber could mean cutting trees, not sawing boards. So it is a guess.

entries.card: notes:SIX FEET, BORROWED FROM THE NEIGHBOURS AND LABELLED AS BORROWED. No source reached states how high this deck stood above the water. The only clearance figure this project holds for any Chicago river crossing of the decade is the 1883 old-settlers statement's 'about six feet above the water' for the two branch bridges, and it is adopted here as an inference from adjacent evidence rather than as evidence about this structure. TWO THINGS SUPPORT THE BORROWING AND ONE COMPLICATES IT. Supporting: the three crossings were built within two years of each other by or for the same corporation, and a bridge that needed a sixty-foot opening for the passage of craft cannot have been high — a high fixed deck is precisely the alternative to a draw, and this town chose the draw. Complicating: the main stem carried masted lake vessels where the branches carried scows and teams, so its bridge had more reason to be built up, and the branch bridges' six feet was set by a use this one did not have, the winter road passing underneath on the ice. The figure is kept because it is the only one there is and because both arguments point low rather than high, and the tag says it is a reading and not a measurement.

entries.card: notes:TEN FEET, AND UNUSUALLY FOR THIS DATASET IT IS SAID TWICE. The 1883 old-settlers statement: 'These bridges were about ten feet wide and without railings, for the first few years.' Both sentences are about BOTH branch bridges, which is what makes this crossing's width evidence rather than an analogy from its neighbour. Cleaver signed the first and gave the second, so the two are one man corroborated by three rather than two independent witnesses; the North Branch record makes the same reservation about the same sentence. Recorded as 3.048 m exactly, being the conversion and not a rounding. The same footnote adds, of the North Branch bridge alone, 'ten or twelve feet wide' — a spread this record does not inherit, because it is stated of the other crossing.

entries.card: notes:THE 1835 READING OF A BRIDGE THAT CHANGED. Andreas describes the 1832 structure as 'formed of stringers and only fitted for foot passengers' and 'useless for teams' even in the summer of 1833; six and a half weeks after this scene's date a procession of hundreds crossed it, and Cleaver remembered driving over it. Something was rebuilt or widened between 1833 and 1835 and no source reached says what. Four stringers under a full-width deck is the later, load-carrying reading, chosen because the scene date is 1835-07-01 and the evidence for 1835 is a crowd on the deck. The alternative — the 1832 walkway, two stringers and a plank — is a defensible model of a different year and would be the right value in an 1833 scene.

levels.8-10: How this bridge looked in 1835, after it changed. A book says the 1832 bridge was made of long logs and fit only for people on foot. Even in the summer of 1833 it was useless for wagons. But six and a half weeks after the day we show, hundreds of people crossed it in a parade, and Cleaver remembered driving over it. So it was rebuilt or made wider between 1833 and 1835. No record says how. Four logs under a full deck is the later, stronger reading. We chose it because the day is 1 July 1835, and the proof for 1835 is a crowd on it. The 1832 walkway, two logs and a board, would be right for a scene of 1833.

entries.card: notes:THE 1835 USE IS ATTESTED, WHICH IS NOT WHAT THIS RECORD EXPECTED TO FIND. Andreas's schools narrative, having just placed George Davis in the Presbyterian church 'later, in 1835', continues: 'John Watkins was THEN teaching what had become a public school on the North Side, on the river bank just east of Clark Street, in the building erected by Colonels Hamilton and Owen.' So the building was in use as a public school in the year of the scene. THE GRAIN IS THE YEAR AND NOT THE DAY, and Andreas adds the limit himself: 'Mr. Watkins taught as late as 1835, but the exact date of his retirement is not known.' A building may stand while its function lapses; here the function is attested for 1835 and cannot be tied to 1 July.

entries.card: notes:THE ATTESTED TRAFFIC IS THE ARGUMENT, AND IT IS ALSO WHY THIS IS NOT A WAGON DOOR. The source drives wagons into the YARD — 'the yard into which the trains were driven' — and puts horses in the STABLE. So what has to get through this building's opening is a horse led in hand, which is what the archetype's 'stable' door is (1.35 m clear); a 2.90 m wagon door would silently move the source's wagon train indoors. NOTE THE ALTERNATIVE, because it is live: a wagon house at a teamsters' inn often had a cart bay at one end, and the outbuilding archetype's own golden case for a hotel stable uses a wagon door. Nothing rules it out and nothing states it, so the smaller opening is recorded.

entries.card: notes:THE BUILD DATE IS DISPUTED, 1834 AGAINST 1835, AND THE DISPUTE IS RESOLVED HERE RATHER THAN LEFT OPEN — but the reasoning matters, because the two dates mean different things for this scene. chicagology reports W. H. Stow, who 'came to Chicago about 1833', saying of his own hotel that 'it was built in 1834'. The hotel chronology says it 'opened in 1835'. 1834 is adopted because it is the BUILDER'S OWN STATEMENT about his own building, recorded with the same detail that gives the 40 ft front, the 60 ft wing and the yard, against an undated one-line entry in a chronology that also mis-sizes the building. THE PHASE MECHANISM WAS CONSIDERED AND DELIBERATELY NOT USED. If the 1835 date were right, the hotel might have been unfinished or brand new on 1835-07-01, and a construction phase would be the honest way to show that. But a construction phase would have to invent a start month, a duration and a state of completeness, none of which any source gives, and it would silently adopt the weaker date to do it. One completed phase on the better-attested date, with the alternative recorded here and in the dossier, claims less. If the 1835 date is ever confirmed, split this phase then. The end of the range is set at the end of 1840, past the last account reached that describes the house in operation; it is not a demolition date and no source reached gives one.

entries.card: notes:THE BUILD YEAR IS DOCUMENTED AND THE MONTH IS NOT, so the range opens at the start of 1827: Andreas, in the packing-house chapter, 'The site of the original log slaughter-house, built by Archibald Clybourne in 1827, for the killing of such cattle as were required by the garrison at Fort Dearborn' (scan p. 1149). THE SURVIVAL TO THE SCENE DATE IS UNUSUALLY WELL SUPPORTED for this dataset: the same building is working six years later — 'The following year [1833] Archibald Clybourne, the Government butcher for the Pottawatomies, engaged in the packing business, at his log slaughter-house on the east side of the North Branch, where he packed some two hundred and fifty head of cattle and about two thousand hogs' (scan p. 1151) — which puts it in full operation nineteen months before 1835-07-01. The range closes at the end of 1835 as the last date this record needs to claim; Andreas writing in 1883 says the site was BY THEN occupied by a later frame slaughter-house of Clybourne's 'now falling into pieces from sheer old age', so the log building came down at some point between 1835 and 1883 and nothing reached dates that.

entries.card: notes:THE DECK, AND NOT ONE OF ITS NUMBERS IS A RECORD'S. Its u extent is the span, 12 m, and its v extent the width, 3 m. THE SPAN IS SIZED OFF THE STREAM, as both its siblings' are: 6.65 m of open water at this northing — 55 % of the span — with 2.60 m and 2.75 m of dry seat left at the two abutments. It is the La Salle crossing's span over a narrower channel, and it is not the Slough Log Bridge's 8 m because 8 m here would leave 0.7 m of seat at each end. THE WIDTH IS THE SMALLEST OF THE THREE AND THAT IS THE ARGUMENT FOR IT. Charles Cleaver's 'these bridges were ten feet wide' (3.05 m) is documented for the two BRANCH bridges and is only a yardstick here; 3.0 m is a hair under it, the same figure the Slough Log Bridge takes, and this crossing has less claim to width than either sibling. It carries North Water Street, whose own record calls its traffic `light` and gives it a 6.0 m track — against South Water Street's 10.5 m, which is what the La Salle crossing's 4.27 m deck answers to. A crossing wider than the road it carries needs is a claim, and nothing here supports one. THIS IS NOT A RIVER BRIDGE AND MUST NOT BE SIZED LIKE ONE: the two branch bridges span 72 m and 56 m; this is a street crossing of a six-metre backwater.

entries.card: notes:THE END OF THIS RANGE IS AN UPPER BOUND, NOT A DATE. The pickets are attested standing in 1831 by someone living inside them - Juliette Kinzie, 'The fort was inclosed by high pickets' - and drawn on the 1830 plan. Robert Fergus, describing the fort in 1850, says 'The whole Fort enclosure was surrounded by a rough-board fence, white-washed, about 6 feet high; the pickets having been removed at an earlier date'. NOTHING REACHED DATES THAT REMOVAL, so the range is closed at the last day before Fergus's view rather than at a real terminus, and the buildings inside carry a longer range than the wall round them for that reason. On 1835-07-01 the post is garrisoned and the pickets stand: the removal belongs to the years after the troops left in December 1836, and a stockade is not pulled down round an occupied garrison.

entries.card: notes:THE ENVELOPE IS ATTESTED AND THE PLAN IS NOT. Original units: 'The front was about forty feet and the wing sixty feet. It was in an L.' 40 ft = 12.19 m and 60 ft = 18.29 m, which is the polygon's bounding box exactly. Areas follow from that and are not attested: about 164 m2 on the ground, 1,770 sq ft. The word 'about' in 'about forty feet' is the source's own. DISPUTED: the hotel chronology calls the Western 'a small structure', which contradicts a 40 by 60 ft two-storey L outright. chicagology's figures are preferred because they come with the builder's account and with the yard and stable description; the chronology gives no dimensions at all, so 'small' is an impression, not a measurement. The stables and yard are attested and are NOT in this polygon.
