entries.card: notes:THE FLAG IS ATTESTED AND ITS PATTERN IS THE LAW'S. Andreas (vol. 1 p. 128) has this staff fly 'a weather-beaten flag'; a garrison staff of the United States flew the national flag. Its star count is not described anywhere reached and is read from the Flag Act of 4 April 1818, which adds a star on the 4th of July after a state's admission: Missouri's (admitted 10 August 1821) made 24 stars on 4 July 1822, and Arkansas's (admitted 15 June 1836) made 25 only on 4 July 1836. So the flag in law on 1 July 1835 has 24 stars and 13 stripes. The arrangement of the stars (four rows of six), the size of the cloth and its wear beyond Andreas's word are reconstructed (L390).

entries.card: notes:THE FLOOR IS THE ADVERTISEMENT, NOT THE BUILDING, AND TWO PAPERS PRINT IT. The Chicago Democrat of 1835-06-10 carries the card over the copy line 'Chicago, June 10, 1835.—8tf' and the Chicago American of 1835-06-13 carries the same card over 'Chicago, June [13], 183[5]'; the Democrat's is the earlier printing and the floor is its date. Both say the subscriber IS NOW OPENING an assortment at these premises, so the trade opens in the second week of June 1835 and the range opens with it. THE BUILDING is necessarily older than the trade in it and no source dates it, so what this range really records is that a clothing and boot store was open at a describable door on South Water Street three weeks before the scene date. THE END IS THE ORDINARY CONTINUITY CUT AT THE SCENE YEAR: the Democrat's file here runs to 1835-08-12 and the American's to 1835-08-29, and nothing reached says when Holbrook left, so 31 December 1835 is this dataset's standing convention and not a reading.

entries.card: notes:THE FORT WAS OCCUPIED ON 1835-07-01 AND THIS PROJECT CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED IT. Andreas gives the sequence: the garrison was withdrawn in 1823, the post was re-garrisoned in October 1828, the troops were removed to Green Bay in May 1831, and 'In June [1832] the fort was once more garrisoned. Major William Whistler being assigned to the command' - held continuously from then until 29 December 1836. For the scene date itself Andreas brackets the command rather than naming it: DeLafayette Wilcox 'commanded until December 18, 1833, and again from September 16, 1835', with 'Major John Bender, Major John Greene and Captain and Brevet-Major Joseph Plympton ... in command at various times' between. The drloihjournal chronology fills the bracket with Maj. John Greene, 5th Infantry, 18 December 1833 to 16 September 1835, which is unfootnoted but lands exactly inside Andreas's two dates. STRENGTH IS NOT ATTESTED for mid-1835; Andreas gives two companies of infantry in 1833 and nothing later, so no number is recorded here. The garrison is why the gates are built shut rather than open and why the fort is modelled maintained rather than decaying.

entries.card: notes:THE FUNCTION IS THE NAME AND EVERY WITNESS USES IT. A United States factory was the government's own trading house — the post at which the Indian trade was carried on the government's account — and all three sources name it as such: the plate letters `U.S. Factor's House`, Hubbard has it occupied 'by a Mr. Jouett, United States factor', and Hurlbut has the American Fur Company buying 'the Factory House' from the United States. WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED IS WHAT WENT ON INSIDE IT IN 1835. The factory system was abolished in 1822, which is the same year Hurlbut has the building sold out of government hands; by the scene date this is a private house that used to be a trading house, and nothing this project holds says whether any trade was still carried on in it.

So the surname is carried, the initial is not, and the record id keeps the H that this project's dossier assigned it because renaming a record is worse than annotating one. Both readings are recorded in aka.

entries.card: notes:THE OPENING IS DISPUTED BY TEN WEEKS AND THE DISPUTE IS BETWEEN THE BUILDER AND HIS COMPILER. Nelson R. Norton, the ship-carpenter who built it, in a letter Andreas prints: 'I came to Chicago November 16, 1833. Soon after I arrived, I commenced cutting the lumber for a drawbridge... In March, 1834, I commenced building it, and I think it was completed by the 1st of June.' Andreas corrects him on the spot: 'Mr. Norton is evidently in error as to the time of the completion of the bridge, since the Democrat states that it was formally accepted by the Trustees in August, the first proposals having been received in February.' The range opens on the LATER of the two, 1 August 1834, because the question a range answers is when the structure certainly stood as a working public crossing, and 'I think it was completed by' is the weaker of the two claims even before Andreas contradicts it. Nothing turns on the choice for this scene: the bridge is standing eleven months before 1835-07-01 either way. THE CLOSE IS THE BEST-ATTESTED DATE ON THIS RECORD: 'the Common Council ordered its removal in July, 1839', and 'a large crowd gathered upon the river before daylight, the next morning, and going to work with a will, in a very short time chopped the bridge to pieces.' A structure destroyed within a day of a dated order is a rarity in this dataset. THE INFERRED TAG IS FOR THE OPENING AND NOT THE CLOSE. The August acceptance rests on an 1834 issue of the Chicago Democrat that this project does not hold, quoted by Andreas fifty years later; the paper itself is the thing that would move this to documented.

entries.card: notes:THE PRICED SERVICE IS THE ARGUMENT. entries.card: notes:THE RANGE HAS ONE WITNESS, NOT TWO, AND THAT IS THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THIS RECORD AND THE OTHER TWO PLACED BESIDE IT. Only the plan names a Shop here; Hubbard walks the same ground on the same two pages and does not mention it. IT OPENS 24 FEBRUARY 1830, the date on the Harrison plan, because that is the earliest date any source this project holds fixes to this building; Hubbard's narrative of the fort's surroundings is of the late 1820s and carries it earlier without dating it. IT CLOSES 29 DECEMBER 1836, the evacuation, and that is a floor rather than a demolition: nothing attests when the fort's outer buildings came down, and a range that ran on to 1856 with the fort's principal structures would claim a survival for a workshop that nobody wrote down. WHAT CARRIES THE SCENE DATE OF 1 JULY 1835 is the middle of that range and not either end of it — the post was garrisoned continuously from June 1832 to 29 December 1836, so a service building the garrison's own engineer drew in 1830 is standing five years later unless something says it stopped, and nothing does. That is an argument, not an assumption, and it is the argument every Fort Dearborn record here rests on.

The tract is real and the register's words about it are read; what is graded here is the claim that THIS roof stands on it, and that claim is the recipe's. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (L219): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.

entries.card: notes:THE SCENE DATE IS BRACKETED BY TWO ATTESTATIONS AND NAMED BY NEITHER. Before it: Andreas, on the Methodist society organised in 1834, 'For a time services were held in various places — in Billy Caldwell's log council-house, in Chester Ingersoll's tavern, or in Watkins's school-house' — a sentence set in 1834, before the congregation's own frame building was contracted on 30 June that year. After it: the Chicago Tribune's account of 18 August 1835, six and a half weeks past the scene date, has the assembly for the last war dance form 'at the "Council House" on the north side of the river'. A building in use in 1834 and in use in August 1835 was standing in between unless something took it down and put it back, which nothing says. THAT INFERENCE IS THE STRONGEST THING IN THIS RECORD AND IT CARRIES A JOIN: Andreas's 'Billy Caldwell's log council-house' and the Tribune's 'Council House' are treated as the same building, on the grounds that both are a council house on the north side in the same two years and neither source knows of a second one. Neither source makes the identification, and if they are two buildings then this record's construction comes from one and its position from the other. The range opens on 1 January 1834 as the earliest day the attested year allows — the treaty council of September 1833 on the same Tribune page mentions 'the council house' too, which may push the building earlier, and the page does not say it is this one — and closes at the end of 1835 as this record's claim horizon.

entries.card: notes:THE SEASON IS DOCUMENTED AND NO EXACT DATE IS. Andreas: 'In the spring of 1833, Tyler K. Blodgett established a brick-yard, on the North Side, not far from the river bank, between Dearborn and Clark streets. He engaged Henry S. Lampman, then of Ann Arbor, as a workman. As Mr. Blodgett operated the first brick-yard in the city, so Mr. Lampman was undoubtedly the first brick-maker' (scan p. 1161). The range opens on 1 March 1833 as the conventional start of spring rather than as a stated date; brickmaking is a summer trade — clay is dug in autumn, weathered over winter, moulded and dried through the warm months — so the yard's first working season is 1833. SURVIVAL TO THE SCENE DATE IS INFERENCE, and it is better supported than most in this dataset: the Lake House, begun on the north bank in 1835, is three storeys and a basement of BRICK, and Andreas's own sentence traces the town's first brick building to this yard, so somebody was making brick in Chicago through the boom. Whether it was still Blodgett on this ground on 1835-07-01 is not attested. The range closes at the end of 1835 as the last date this record needs to claim.

entries.card: notes:THE SOURCE OFFERS TWO YEARS AND THIS RANGE TAKES THE LATER ONE AS A FLOOR. Andreas: 'a wooden structure, erected in 1833 or 1834, by John Bates, for an auction-room.' The range opens at the start of 1834, the later of the two; if Andreas meant 1833 the building is a year older than this says, and if he meant late 1834 the range opens a few months early. Neither reading changes the 1835 scene, which is why the ambiguity is recorded rather than resolved. Bates is independently attested as the auctioneer for the school-section sale of October 1833 and as an active advertiser in 1834, and he was deputy postmaster from 1833, so the man is well placed in the town on either date. THE END IS THE ORDINARY CONTINUITY CUT AT THE SCENE YEAR; no source reached follows the building past its erection.

entries.card: notes:THE START DATE DEPENDS ON WHICH BUILDING THIS IS, WHICH IS THE SAME DISPUTE AS THE POSITION. Wau-Bun describes the log school-house standing at Wolf Point in 1831, and the first Methodist society was organised on 14 June 1831 with ten members in a log cabin, so 1831 is the start under the reading adopted here. Under the competing reading the building standing in 1835 is a cabin the congregation BUILT IN 1834 on the other bank, in which case this range begins three years too early. The end is firmer: the congregation floated the cabin across the river in 1838 and rolled it on logs to Washington and Clark, which ends the phase wherever it began — and is itself the reason phases carry their own position in this schema. Tagged inferred rather than documented because the start rests on identifying the 1835 building with the 1831 one.

entries.card: notes:THE START IS DOCUMENTED TO THE DAY, WHICH IS RARE IN THIS DATASET. Andreas: 'It was upon the eighth day of October, 1833, that a young man named Asahel Pierce arrived in Chicago from Vermont, and commenced the erection of a blacksmith shop, on Lake Street, corner of Canal' (scan p. 1161). The range opens on that date, which is when building BEGAN rather than when the shop was working — nothing says how long it took, and a small board shop is a matter of weeks. The range is tagged inferred rather than documented for the far end only: nothing reached follows the building past 1834, and it closes at the end of 1835 as the last date this record needs to claim. THE SURVIVAL IS BETTER SUPPORTED THAN MOST HERE: Andreas has Pierce ironing the first Chicago-to-St-Louis stage line for John T. Temple & Co. in January 1834 and beginning the manufacture of the old-fashioned 'Bull' plough with a wooden mould-board in the spring of that year, which is a business growing rather than folding, and Pierce is still a Chicago figure decades later, an alderman in 1843 and 1844 with two streets named after him (scan pp. 387, 411).

entries.card: notes:THE YEAR IS ATTESTED AND THE MONTH IS NOT, so the range opens on 1 January 1831 rather than claiming a build date. Andreas, independently and with a direction the other source lacks: 'John Miller, brother of Samuel, the landlord, came in 1831, and run a tannery just north of Miller's tavern.' THE END OF THE RANGE IS THE HONEST MINIMUM, NOT A FATE. Nothing reached follows this building past its founding: Andreas adds a partner, 'Benjamin Hall, tanner, a partner of John Miller, who came in 1832', and then the trade drops out of the record, while Samuel Miller — the brother whose tavern fixes this building's position — 'sold the tavern and moved away following the death of his wife in 1832'. So the anchor moved on three years before the scene date and the tannery's own survival rests on the ordinary continuity argument: a standing building stands until something says otherwise. Tagged inferred for that reason.

entries.card: notes:THE YEAR IS ATTESTED, THE MONTH IS NOT, AND THE BUILDING ITSELF IS DISPUTED BY THE MAN WHO TAUGHT IN IT. Andreas: 'It is stated in Mr. Wells's report that these gentlemen [Colonels Hamilton and Owen] afterwards built a house on the north bank of the river, just east of Clark Street, in which Mr. Watkins continued his school, and that it was the first house built for a school in Chicago. BUT THIS DOES NOT RECUR TO MR. WATKINS'S RECOLLECTION.' Andreas prints the doubt and then, forty pages later, states the building as fact and dates it: 'John Watkins was then teaching what had become a public school on the North Side, on the river bank just east of Clark Street, in the building erected by Colonels Hamilton and Owen, as has already been stated, in 1833.' A THIRD PASSAGE CORROBORATES A SCHOOL BUILDING THERE, independently of Wells: Andreas's Methodist chapter has Jesse Walker's first quarterly meeting held 'in the Watkins school-house, which was located on North Water Street, between Clark and LaSalle'. So a Watkins school-house existed on North Water Street near Clark in 1834, whatever Watkins remembered about who built it. The range opens on 1 January 1833 as the earliest day the attested year allows and closes at the end of 1835 as this record's claim horizon; no source follows the building past Watkins, who 'taught as late as 1835, but the exact date of his retirement is not known'.

entries.card: notes:THE YEAR IS DOCUMENTED AND THE MONTH IS NOT. Andreas, in the packing-house chapter: 'In 1834, Oliver Newberry and George W. Dole had a slaughter-house erected on the South Branch of the river, where some three hundred head of cattle and fourteen hundred hogs were packed during the year' (scan p. 1151). The range therefore opens at the start of 1834 for want of a month; packing is winter work, so the plant was probably up by the autumn of that year rather than in January, and the phrase 'during the year' means the 1834 season. THE SURVIVAL TO 1835-07-01 IS ORDINARY CONTINUITY AND IS NOT ATTESTED — nothing reached follows this building past its first season. What can be said for it is that a purpose-built plant which handled 300 cattle and 1,400 hogs in its first year was not abandoned within eighteen months, and that the firm was still trading in Chicago through the decade. The range closes at the end of 1835 as the last date this record needs to claim.

entries.card: notes:THE YEAR IS DOCUMENTED TWICE IN ANDREAS AND THE MONTH IS NOT. In his hotel chapter: 'Mr. Beaubien had meanwhile built a new house on the northwest corner of Wells and Lake streets. In August of 1834, Mr. and Mrs. Murphy took charge of this new hotel, which they christened the Exchange Coffee House.' In his life of Mark Beaubien: 'In the latter year [1834] he completed another house on the northwest corner of Wells and Lake streets, which was called the Exchange Coffee House, and first kept by Mr. and Mrs. John Murphy.' So the house was finished and trading by August 1834, eleven months before the scene date, and 1834-01-01 is the first day the attested year permits rather than a date anybody gives - which is why this range is inferred and not documented. THE SCENE DATE IS NOT AT RISK: whatever month in 1834 the building went up, it was open under the Murphys from August 1834 and they 'remained there until 1836'. THE END IS A BOUND WHERE THE EVIDENCE STOPS, NOT A DEMOLITION: the Murphys left for the old Sauganash in 1836 and this project has nothing dating the building's fate. Andreas's list of minor houses in 1845 includes 'the Illinois Exchange, corner Wells and Lake streets', which may be the same fabric under a later sign or may not; the phase is closed at the end of the attested tenancy rather than run on speculatively.

entries.card: notes:THIS RANGE IS ANDREAS'S DESCRIPTIVE WINDOW, NOT THE STAFF'S LIFE. His section 'Chicago from 1833 to 1837' opens at the close of 1833 with the town legally organized and describes what a visitor saw across those four years; the flagstaff sentence sits in that description. Nothing reached says when the staff was raised or when it came down, so the range is set to the window of the only text that puts it there and both ends are limits of the SOURCE rather than of the object. The scene date sits comfortably inside it. The obvious candidate for a real end - 29 December 1836, when the troops were permanently withdrawn under a printed order - is deliberately NOT used: it dates the garrison, not the spar, and the buildings stood into the 1850s.

entries.card: notes:TWO READINGS THAT DO NOT AGREE, AND THIS RECORD TAKES THE STATED ONE. The 1855 key gives 'the Officers' Quarters, B (wood, about 30x60 ft,)' - 9.14 x 18.29 m, which is the polygon here. The 1830 plan draws the west range about 30 ft deep and about 80 ft long at the scale this project derives, so the two agree on the depth to within 3 percent and disagree on the length by nearly 40 percent. THE STATED FIGURE WINS, and the reasoning is worth writing down because it decides several records: the scale that would overrule it was itself calibrated on the other stated figure in the same caption, so using it to correct that caption's second number is close to circular. What that costs is legible - the modelled building is about 6 m shorter than the plan draws its range - and it is why this footprint is inferred while the commandant's is documented. If the 1830 plan is right the officers were housed in an 80 ft range; if the 1855 caption is right they were in a 60 ft one; nothing reached settles it.

entries.card: notes:The Clybournes lived on this ground and butchered from it: Andreas has Jonas Clybourne living several miles up the North Branch among the county's taxpayers (scan p. 215) and 'Jonas Clybourne and his son Archibald were the early butchers of Chicago. They furnished the garrison at Fort Dearborn' (scan p. 221). So the cabins are a farmstead at the head of a stock-raising and butchering business rather than town houses, and that is an inference from the family's trade rather than a description of the buildings. Who was living in them on 1835-07-01 is not attested and this record carries no occupants block: Archibald had a larger house of his own from 1829, and the household's composition eleven years after the cabins went up is not recorded anywhere reached.

Our old note said the tall part stood in front of the cabin, from the words facing the river. But those words tell which way it faced, not where it stood. The old note mixed that up. The side by side shape comes from the picture. Its exact sizes, and that it was so in July 1835, are graded on their own. It still faces the river.

entries.card: notes:The closed vocabulary has no `stock shed`; `stable` is family A1's own term and the nearest it carries. The specific use - holding beasts before the kill, and the plant's own draught oxen - is in the record's NAME and in this note. The use comes from the plant. A slaughter-house that took 300 head of cattle and 1,400 hogs in a season held stock somewhere before it killed them, and the plant's own record says the pens and the stock yard are outside its footprint and outside its archetype. This record models the roofed half of that; the pens themselves are a fence line and this archetype builds buildings. No occupant is claimed and no animal is drawn.

The pens are a fence line, and we build buildings. No one is placed in it, and no animal is drawn.

A picture in Andreas's 1884 book shows a pointed roof that slopes on all sides. We keep that as a place where the two pictures do not agree. Using the 1902 picture for July 1835 is our choice. It does not claim the picture shows July.

entries.card: notes:The dossier groups this building with Newberry & Dole's as one of the two river warehouses with docks, which puts it in the forwarding and commission trade by association rather than by statement — no source reached says what Kinzie & Hunter forwarded. Andreas has a firm of Kinzie, Hunter & Co. in the LUMBER trade in the middle 1830s, taking it up a couple of years after the first cargo of pine was landed on the south bank between LaSalle and Wells (scan p. 1139), so a lumber yard rather than a general warehouse is a live alternative reading of what this building was for. Recorded as inference with the alternative named.

levels.8-10: Our notes put this building with Newberry and Dole's, as one of two store houses on the river with docks. That makes it a shipping house by being next to one, not because a record says so. No record says what Kinzie and Hunter shipped. A book says a firm of Kinzie, Hunter and Co. sold wood in the middle 1830s. So a wood yard, not a store house, is another real answer. We record it as our guess, and name the other one.

entries.card: notes:The dossier's sentence says log cabins, and it is unattributed; the family's own slaughter-house on the same ground is twice called log in Andreas (scan pp. 1149, 1151), and every settler dwelling on the branches in the 1820s that any source describes is log. So the material is inference resting on the neighbourhood and on the same household's other building, not on a statement this project can point at. If the dossier's sentence is ever traced to its source this becomes documented without anything else in the record moving.

levels.8-10: Our notes say log cabins, but do not say where that came from. A book twice says the family's butcher house on the same land was made of logs. Every settler home on the river's branches in the 1820s that any record tells of was logs. So logs is a guess from the houses nearby and the family's other building. If we ever find where our note came from, this becomes a fact.

The board sizes and the sides no one sees are our guesses. A picture made years later does not settle how it looked in July 1835.

entries.card: notes:The identification of the partners is the dossier's and rests on the surname pairing: John H. Kinzie and Lieutenant Hunter came to Chicago together in February 1833 to lay out lots through their property north of the river, and both are among the backers of the Lake House in 1835. Its midpoint at 2.6 m is a reconstructed floor/cladding break; the board-edge rhythm, narrow relief and exact joint treatment are reconstructed proxies under L-miller-mixed-cladding-2381. ACTUAL-RENDER FOLLOW-UP: the first same-material 12 mm edge/12 mm relief treatment was visually ineffective. Joint proxies now use 24 mm width and 4 mm relief with the existing darker log material, at the retained nominal 0.24 m board rhythm. entries.card: notes:The weather pier of the federal harbour improvement: the northern of the two piers that hold open the 1834 cut through the sand bar, keeping the littoral drift out of the entrance and the channel scoured. It is the reason there is a harbour at Chicago at all — before it the river turned south behind the bar and lake vessels anchored half a mile offshore and lightered their cargo. Congress appropriated $25,000 for the work on 2 March 1833; the schooner Illinois came through the cut on 12 July 1834, the first vessel to enter the river; the appropriation for 1835 was $32,800. By the scene date Chicago is the leading port in the West and this structure is why.

levels.8-10: The north pier of the country's harbor work. It is the north one of two piers that hold open the 1834 cut through the sand bar. It keeps the drifting sand out and the channel clear. It is the reason there is a harbor at Chicago at all. Before it, the river turned south behind the sand bar. Ships stopped half a mile out, and small boats carried their goods in. Congress gave $25,000 for the work in March 1833. The schooner Illinois came through the cut on 12 July 1834, the first ship into the river. In 1835 Congress gave $32,800 more. By the day we show, Chicago is the busiest port in the West, and this pier is why.

entries.card: notes:V3 SOLID-CRIB TRIAL, retained as history: TWO BROAD DRAW-BEARING PLATFORMS. The retrospective Andreas plate shows broad foundations under the gallows rather than a forest of identical narrow box cribs. The two selected bearing cribs use a reconstructed 3.6 m nominal box length away from the draw and 4.4 m width across it. These are bounded visual-trial dimensions, not a survey, geographic footprint or historical specification; visible log joints project slightly beyond that box. Existing draw endpoints and the twelve support stations remain unchanged. The remaining approaches use separately reconstructed timber bents; whole source comparison stays differs. CURRENT PILED-CAP CORRECTION: direct inspection of the complete 1920 px plate shows a boarded cap over closely spaced vertical piles, not a solid horizontal-log crib. The selected 3.6 m along by 6.0 m across platform is centered on each existing frame bearing. Its 0.30 m diameter perimeter piles at at most 0.48 m spacing, two 0.20 m sleepers, 0.14 m boarded cap and below-water stopping depth are reconstructed visual choices, not dimensions or a foundation count attested by the retrospective drawing. Keep the reconstructed 3.6 m along-bearing plan and -1.0 m transverse offset. The foundation dimensions and resulting 46 perimeter piles, formerly 38, remain reconstructed construction choices. levels.8-10: Three people wrote about these houses. Wau-Bun calls them a group of log buildings. Andreas calls them small log buildings. McKee, who built houses here in 1823, said they were all made of logs. Logs are the one thing all three agree on.

entries.card: notes:Wau-Bun calls them cabins 'occupied by' named people and later refers to the group as 'these residences'. They were homes.

entries.card: notes:Wau-Bun counts them loosely — 'two or three' — and the looseness is the evidence, so the value is kept as the source's words rather than resolved to a number. ONE CABIN IS BUILT. The archetype models a building, not a group, and choosing two or three would mean inventing the count the source declined to give, plus their spacing and their arrangement. So the model understates the place: a visitor sees one cabin where there were at least two, and the record says so here.

An old drawing shows the big front roof and a smaller side roof. It can't show the back or where the roofs meet, so all of that is our guess.

entries.card: notes:Wau-Bun describes the buildings round the agency house as 'a collection of log buildings, the residences of the different persons in the employ of Government ... blacksmith, striker, and laborers'; Andreas records the 1830 north bank as having 'small log buildings occupied by the blacksmith, Mr. McKee, and Billy Caldwell' in the agency house's vicinity, and McKee's own account of the houses he found and built there — 'All these houses were of logs'. Note that the first two describe the blacksmith's RESIDENCE among the group; that the shop was of the same fabric is the reading, and it is the only fabric anybody reports on this ground in these years.

Note that the first two describe the blacksmith's RESIDENCE among the group; that the shop was of the same fabric is the reading, and it is the only fabric anybody reports on this ground in these years.

levels.8-10: Wau-Bun says the buildings near the Agency House were log homes for the government's workers, the blacksmith among them. Andreas says the same of 1830, naming McKee. McKee himself said all the houses there were logs. But those writers tell of the blacksmith's home. That his shop was logs too is our guess. Logs are the only kind of wall anyone saw here then.

entries.card: notes:Wau-Bun names the OFFICE among the residences and not the building: 'Around the Agency House were grouped a collection of log buildings, the residences of the different persons in the employ of Government ... blacksmith, striker, and laborers.' That the striker had one of the residences is what that sentence says; that it was a separate building rather than a room in the blacksmith's is the inference. Graded below the other two houses of this parcel for that reason.

So the striker had a home. That it was its own house, not a room in the blacksmith's, is our guess. So we trust it less than the other two houses here.

levels.8-10: Wau-Bun, telling of 1831, says a house just finished by Mark Beaubien. It burned down on 4 March 1851. It was renamed the Chicago Hotel in 1838. A theater company used the dining room in 1837. Those changed its use, not its shape, so they do not start a new stage.

entries.card: notes:Wau-Bun: 'a pretentious white two-story building, with bright-blue wooden shutters.' Painted white siding was itself remarkable at Wolf Point in 1831 — the description exists because the building stood out.
entries.text: Wau-Bun: 'a pretentious white two-story building, with bright-blue wooden shutters.' Painted white siding was itself remarkable at Wolf Point in 1831 — the description exists because the building stood out.

levels.8-10: Wau-Bun calls it a showy white building of two floors, with bright blue wood shutters. White paint was itself special at Wolf Point in 1831. The book tells of it because the building stood out.

Andreas, recording David McKee's account of the north side when he arrived in 1823: 'All these houses were of logs — the agency-house being afterward clapboarded part way up.' Hewn and squared log is exactly what this archetype builds. The clapboarding is recorded separately under `cladding`, with its unknown extent and date kept explicit there.

levels.8-10: Wau-Bun calls it a solid, compact little building of logs, cut and squared. McKee, who came in 1823, said all the houses there were logs. He said the agency house later got boards part way up its walls. Cut and squared logs is just what we build. The boards are kept in a separate note, since how far up they went, and when, are not known.
